analogy.p: Picture a hall of students. In a **solid** they stand shoulder to shoulder in rows, only swaying on the spot. In a **liquid** it is a crowded corridor: everyone is still touching but they can shuffle past each other. In a **gas** it is an open field at break time: students run about far apart, bumping only occasionally. The more energy the students have (heating), the more they move, until they break free of their rows. It breaks down because real particles attract each other with forces, whereas students only avoid each other, and all students are the same speed in the picture.

bullets: The model explains **why** a solid keeps its shape (strong forces hold particles in fixed positions) and **why** a gas can be squashed (huge gaps between particles).
The **forces of attraction** between particles are called **intermolecular forces** (or bonds in the model); stronger forces hold the particles closer together.
The particles are in constant motion in every state: in solids they **vibrate about fixed positions**, in liquids and gases they move from place to place.
The same substance in different states is made of the **same particles**; only the arrangement, spacing and energy differ.
Heating gives particles more **kinetic energy**, so they move or vibrate faster and push each other further apart.
Always link the state to **arrangement, movement and forces** in an exam answer, as all three are credited.
core.p: All matter is made of tiny **particles** (atoms or molecules) that are always moving. The **particle model** pictures these particles as small solid spheres, and uses their **arrangement**, **movement** and the **forces between them** to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases. The three states differ because of how strongly the particles attract each other compared with how much kinetic energy they have.

bullets: **Arrangement:** regular (a lattice), closely packed and touching.
**Movement:** vibrate about fixed positions; more vibration as temperature rises.
**Forces:** strong, so the particles cannot escape their neighbours.
**Properties:** fixed shape, fixed volume, very hard to compress, generally the highest density.
**Why hard to compress:** there is almost no space between particles to squash into.
**Why they expand when heated:** bigger vibrations push particles very slightly further apart.
**Exam phrase:** 'particles vibrate about fixed positions in a regular arrangement'.
core.p: In a **solid** the particles are held very close together in a **regular, fixed pattern** by strong forces of attraction. They cannot move from place to place, but they **vibrate about fixed positions**. Because the particles cannot slide past each other, a solid has a **fixed shape and fixed volume** and cannot flow or be easily compressed.

bullets: **Arrangement:** random, close together, mostly touching.
**Movement:** particles move around and slide past each other in all directions.
**Properties:** fixed volume, no fixed shape, flows, very hard to compress.
**Compared with solids:** particles have more kinetic energy and the forces are weaker relative to that energy, so the lattice breaks down.
**Density:** usually slightly lower than the solid, because particles are slightly further apart. Water is unusual: ice is **less dense** than liquid water, which is why ice floats.
**Diffusion** is possible because particles move, but slow because of the crowding.
core.p: In a **liquid** the particles are still **close together and touching**, but the arrangement is **random** and the particles can **move past each other**. The forces of attraction are still strong enough to keep the particles together, so a liquid has a fixed volume, but they are not strong enough to hold the particles in fixed positions, so a liquid takes the shape of its container and can flow.

bullets: **Arrangement:** random, widely spaced; the particles occupy only a tiny fraction of the volume.
**Movement:** rapid, random motion in straight lines, changing direction only on collision.
**Forces:** very weak or none between collisions.
**Properties:** no fixed shape or volume, easily compressed, flows, very low density (typically about 1000 times less dense than a liquid).
**Pressure:** caused by particles colliding with the container walls, each collision exerting a tiny force.
**Higher temperature:** faster particles, so more frequent and harder collisions and, in a fixed volume, a higher pressure.
core.p: In a **gas** the particles are **far apart** with **random** positions, moving **quickly in straight lines** until they collide with each other or the container walls. The forces between particles are **negligible** (almost zero), so a gas has **no fixed shape or volume** and spreads out to fill any container. The huge gaps mean a gas can be compressed easily and has a very low density.

bullets: **Melting:** solid to liquid. Happens at the **melting point**, a fixed temperature for a pure substance (0 °C for pure water).
**Freezing:** liquid to solid at the same temperature as melting (the **freezing point**).
**Boiling:** liquid to gas **throughout the whole liquid**, with bubbles of vapour forming, at the **boiling point** (100 °C for pure water at normal pressure).
**Evaporating:** liquid to gas **at the surface only**, at any temperature below the boiling point, with no bubbles.
**Condensing:** gas to liquid on cooling (steam forming water droplets on a cold window).
**Sublimating:** solid straight to gas **without passing through the liquid state** (dry ice, solid carbon dioxide, or iodine crystals).
The reverse of sublimation (gas straight to solid, as in frost) is called **deposition**; it is not named in the AQA list but is the same idea in reverse.
Melting and boiling are **endothermic** (energy taken in); freezing and condensing are **exothermic** (energy given out to the surroundings).
core.p: A **change of state** happens when a substance turns from one state to another. The AQA specification names **melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating**. Heating (energy transferred **to** the substance) takes you from solid to liquid to gas; cooling (energy transferred **from** the substance) reverses this. Learn the direction of each one and the key definition.

bullets: During melting and boiling, **energy is transferred to the substance but the temperature stays constant**.
The energy increases the **potential energy** of the particles (moving them further apart against the attractive forces), not their average kinetic energy.
The average kinetic energy of the particles is what determines the **temperature**, so with kinetic energy constant, temperature is constant.
During freezing and condensing, new attractions form and **energy is released** to the surroundings; the temperature again stays constant until the change is complete.
The amount of energy needed per kilogram to change state is the **specific latent heat** (a separate spec point).
**Link:** this is why a gas has much higher internal energy than the same mass of the liquid at the same temperature.
core.h: Why changes of state happen: energy and bonds
core.p: When a solid is heated, the particles gain **kinetic energy** and vibrate more. At the melting point the vibrations are strong enough that the particles can break free from their fixed positions, and the **energy supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction** between particles. The same applies at boiling, where the particles gain enough energy to separate completely. While this happens the **temperature does not rise** because energy is going into breaking bonds (increasing potential energy) rather than increasing kinetic energy.

bullets: **Sloping section:** the substance is in one state and its temperature rises; energy goes into **kinetic energy** of particles.
**Flat section:** a change of state; energy goes into **breaking bonds** (potential energy); the substance is a **mixture of two states**.
**Read the melting point** from the first plateau and the **boiling point** from the second.
**Steeper slope** means the temperature rises faster per unit energy, i.e. a lower specific heat capacity for that state (gas and solid warm faster than liquid water).
**Length of plateau** shows how much energy is needed: boiling plateau is longer than melting because separating particles completely needs more energy.
An **impure substance** melts or boils over a **range** of temperatures, so there is no flat plateau; a pure substance has a sharp, fixed point.
On a cooling curve, the plateaux happen at the same temperatures, but energy is leaving the substance.
core.p: A **heating curve** plots temperature (y-axis) against time or energy supplied (x-axis) for a substance heated steadily. It consists of **sloping sections**, where a single state warms up, and **flat sections (plateaux)**, where a change of state occurs. The temperature of each plateau is the **melting point** or **boiling point**. Cooling curves are the same graph reversed, with plateaux at the freezing and condensing points.

bullets: **Evaporation:** the particles that escape are the **most energetic**, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid falls and the liquid **cools**.
**Faster evaporation** with higher temperature, larger surface area, moving air (removes vapour particles that would return) and low humidity.
**Boiling** occurs when the liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so bubbles can form and grow; do not use this phrase unless asked for more detail.
Boiling needs a **continuous energy supply**; evaporation can occur without a heater, taking energy from the surroundings.
**Exam link:** sweat evaporating cools the body because the fastest particles leave, lowering the average kinetic energy of the sweat and skin.
core.p: Both processes turn a liquid into a gas, but they happen differently. **Evaporation** occurs only at the **surface** and at **any temperature** below the boiling point, when the fastest-moving particles near the surface have enough kinetic energy to escape the attraction of the other particles. **Boiling** happens at one particular temperature, throughout the whole liquid, when bubbles of vapour form inside it.

bullets: Melt ice to water and refreeze it: you get **ice with the same properties** as at the start, so it is a physical change.
The **particles themselves do not change**: a water molecule is still H2O in ice, water and steam.
Only the **arrangement, spacing and energy** of the particles change.
**Chemical change:** bonds within molecules are broken and made, giving new substances (burning methane makes carbon dioxide and water).
Physical changes are usually **reversible** simply by heating or cooling; many chemical changes are not easily reversible.
**Exam phrase:** 'it is a physical change because no new substance is formed and the original properties are recovered when the change is reversed'.
core.p: Changes of state are **physical changes**. In a physical change **no new substance is made**; the material **recovers its original properties if the change is reversed**. This is the AQA wording to learn. A chemical change (such as burning or rusting) makes new substances with different properties, and the change is not simply undone by cooling or heating.

bullets: 250 g of ice melts to give **250 g** of water.
**Volume often changes** (a gas occupies far more volume than the liquid it came from), so the **density changes**, but not the mass.
In an open container a liquid that evaporates seems to 'lose mass' because the vapour escapes into the air; in a **sealed** container the total mass stays the same.
This is a **physical change** and **conservation of mass** applies to chemical changes as well (the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products).
**Density = mass ÷ volume** links to this: constant mass, changing volume gives changing density.
Water is unusual: when it freezes its volume **increases** (about 9%), so ice is less dense than water.
core.p: During a change of state, **mass is conserved**. The number of particles does not change and the particles are not destroyed or created, so the mass before equals the mass after. The **volume** and **density** can change, but the mass cannot. This is a commonly examined idea because students confuse mass with volume.

bullets: Particles are shown as **solid spheres with no internal structure**, but real atoms and molecules have different shapes and sizes.
The **forces between particles** are not shown in the diagrams, so the model cannot easily show the strength of attractions.
Diagrams show the **spacing** in a gas as close together on paper, whereas in reality the gaps are enormous compared with the particle size.
Diagrams are **static**; they cannot show that particles are constantly moving or their speeds.
Despite this, the model **successfully explains** changes of state, density, diffusion and gas pressure.
core.p: Like all models, the particle model is a simplification. It treats particles as **hard, solid spheres** and ignores some real features. Examiners may ask you to evaluate it, so know a few specific limitations.

bullets: **Internal energy (4.3.2):** internal energy is the total kinetic plus potential energy of the particles; during a change of state the **potential energy** changes.
**Specific latent heat:** E = m L gives the energy for a change of state without a temperature change.
**Gas pressure (4.3.3):** explained with particle collisions on the walls of the container.
**Chemistry (Paper 1/2 Chemistry):** states of matter, purification by distillation (evaporation and condensation) and crystallisation.
**Energy (4.1):** heating a substance is an energy transfer that changes the thermal store.
core.p: Changes of state tie together several parts of the specification. Mentioning these links in longer answers shows examiners you understand the big picture. **Density (4.3.1):** density depends on how closely the particles are packed; a change of state changes the volume, hence the density.

exam: **1 mark** questions ask for a definition or a state name, e.g. 'name the change from solid to gas' (sublimating). Use the exact word.
**2 mark** 'describe the arrangement and movement' questions: one mark for arrangement (regular / random, close / far apart) and one for movement (vibrate / move past / move quickly and randomly).
**'Explain' questions** need a reason: 'because the particles gain enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them'.

**Heating curve questions:** state the temperature of the plateau for a melting or boiling point, and say 'the energy is used to break bonds (change the potential energy), not to raise the temperature'.
**4 mark questions** on a heating curve: identify each section, say which state(s) are present, say what happens to the particles' energy and why the temperature is constant on a plateau.

**6 mark extended answers:** compare solids, liquids and gases (arrangement, movement, forces, properties) and then link to energy; use a logical order and the key words 'kinetic energy', 'potential energy' and 'forces of attraction'.
**Physical versus chemical:** the mark scheme phrase is 'no new substance is made' and 'the original properties are recovered'.
**Mass or volume?** If asked about mass after a change of state, say 'mass is conserved' and state the same number with units.
**Graphs:** label axes with quantity and unit, read plateaux carefully and use a ruler.
**Command words:** 'describe' = what happens; 'explain' = why (use 'because'); 'compare' = similarities and differences with both sides stated.

mistakes.r: The temperature stays constant. The energy supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles (increasing potential energy).
mistakes.w: During melting the particles get hotter and move faster.

mistakes.r: The particles do not change size or melt. Their spacing, arrangement and speed change.
mistakes.w: The particles themselves melt, expand or get bigger when heated.

mistakes.r: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions.
mistakes.w: Particles in a solid do not move.

mistakes.r: Evaporation is at the surface at any temperature below boiling; boiling is throughout the liquid at the boiling point with bubbles.
mistakes.w: Boiling and evaporation are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Mass is conserved; the number of particles is the same. Only the volume and density change.
mistakes.w: Mass decreases when a liquid turns to gas.

mistakes.r: It is a physical change: no new substance, and the original properties return on refreezing.
mistakes.w: Melting is a chemical change because the ice becomes water.

mistakes.r: Only the intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome; each molecule stays as H2O.
mistakes.w: The bonds in the water molecule break when water boils.

mistakes.r: They are the same particles; in a gas they are far apart with more kinetic energy and negligible forces between them.
mistakes.w: Gas particles are bigger or hotter than liquid particles.

summary: AQA 4.3 requires you to describe, using the particle model, how a substance changes between solid, liquid and gas (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating), to explain that these are physical changes that are reversible and conserve mass, and to link them to energy transfer. It matters because it underpins density, specific latent heat, gas pressure and almost every 'explain using particles' question on Paper 1.

terms.d: A model in which matter is made of small particles whose arrangement, movement and the forces between them explain properties of solids, liquids and gases.
A physical change in which a substance changes between solid, liquid and gas.
Change from solid to liquid at the melting point.
Change from liquid to solid at the freezing point.
Change from liquid to gas throughout the liquid, with bubbles, at the boiling point.
Change from liquid to gas at the surface of the liquid, at any temperature below the boiling point.
Change from gas to liquid as the substance is cooled.
Change directly from solid to gas without becoming a liquid.
A change in which no new substance is formed and the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.
A change in which new substances are formed by the making and breaking of chemical bonds.
The fixed temperature at which a pure solid changes to a liquid.
The fixed temperature at which a pure liquid changes to a gas throughout the liquid.
The total mass is the same before and after a change; mass is neither created nor destroyed.
Attractive forces between particles; they must be overcome during melting and boiling.
Energy of particles due to their movement; the average value determines the temperature.
The flat part of a heating or cooling curve where the temperature is constant during a change of state.
Mass per unit volume of a substance, in kg/m3 or g/cm3.

worked.ans: Energy supplied is used to overcome the forces holding the particles in fixed positions, so the regular arrangement is lost and the particles can move past each other. The temperature stays at 0 °C because the energy increases the potential energy of the particles, not their average kinetic energy.
worked.q: Describe, in terms of particles, what happens as ice at 0 °C is heated until it has all become water at 0 °C. (4 marks)
steps: Energy is transferred to the ice, so the particles gain energy.
The energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles.
The regular arrangement breaks down, and particles can move past one another.
The temperature stays constant because the energy increases potential energy, not the average kinetic energy.

worked.ans: Water mass = 500 g; volume of water = 500 cm3; volume of the ice = 543 cm3.
worked.q: 500 g of ice (density 0.92 g/cm3) melts into water (density 1.00 g/cm3). Calculate the mass and volume of the water and the volume of the ice. (4 marks)
steps: Mass is conserved, so the water has a mass of 500 g.
Volume of ice = mass ÷ density = 500 ÷ 0.92 = 543 cm3 (to 3 s.f.).
The volume decreases by about 43 cm3 as the ice melts.

worked.ans: The faster, more energetic particles leave the surface of the sweat, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining sweat falls and the body cools. Wind carries away vapour so more particles escape and evaporation is faster.
worked.q: Explain why sweat cools the body and why this works better on a windy day. (3 marks)
steps: The most energetic particles escape, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid falls (it cools).
Wind removes the vapour particles near the skin so fewer return, and evaporation is faster.
